aic:110663.texto:
For this frenetic scene, Eugène Delacroix took inspiration from “The Giaour,” a poem in a popular series of romantic tales by the celebrated English poet Lord Byron. Giaour is a derogatory Turkish word for a Christian or non-Muslim applied here to the warrior at left clad in swirling white drapery. Amid a violent struggle, the Giaour is avenging the death of his lover at the hands of his opponent. Delacroix mirrored the two central figures and their horses as the Giaour is about to strike the fatal blow against the faceless Turk Hassan. The artist’s mastery of color is exemplified by his use of shimmering primary hues, while the loose handling of paint creates the sense of dynamism Delacroix was so capable of executing.
This painting reflects Delacroix’s sustained engagement with Orientalism, the artistic representation of non-European people and places, especially North Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. Delacroix was among the first European artists to travel to Africa when he visited Morocco in 1832, shortly after he completed this painting. Widespread in the nineteenth century, Orientalism was regularly leveraged to reinforce French colonial enterprises through often fantastical, violent, or erotic depictions of the customs and cultures of faraway locales.
aic:110663.title: The Combat of the Giaour and Hassan

aic:152851.texto: This is a preparatory sketch for a monumental painting depicting one of the bloodiest moments of Napoleon’s 1798 invasion of Egypt: the suppression of an uprising in Cairo. The conflict included a massacre in the Al-Azhar Mosque of Mamelukes, a military class of enslaved men who occupied much of the Middle East at that time. As there were no surviving eyewitness reports, Girodet was free to interpret the event as he wished, and, as a commission from Napoleon, the painting celebrates the French point of view. Throughout the work, Girodet perpetuates European fantasies of the Middle East as simultaneously opulent and brutal, lavishing attention on Arab and Ottoman turbans, luxurious fabrics, bare flesh, and gore.
aic:152851.title: Sketch for The Revolt of Cairo

cma:146725.texto: In 1810, Gros exhibited a massive painting of Napoleon at the 1798 Battle of the Pyramids, one of the rare French triumphs in the failed campaign to conquer Egypt (1789-1801). After Napoleon first fell from power in 1814, the painting went into storage, until the new king Louis-Philippe chose to resurrect it for a history museum in Paris. However, perhaps to diminish Napoleon's significance, the government asked Gros to amplify the original with an addition at each end. This painting incorporates General Kléber, a famously successful military leader who had been excluded from the original painting.
cma:146725.title: General Jean-Baptiste Kléber and Egyptian Family (Sketches for "The Battle of the Pyramids")

cma:150080.texto: In 1809, the popular young French military hero General Auguste Colbert died at a battle in Spain. The following year, Schnetz depicted the moment of Colbert's death. This is the study for a much larger painting exhibited at the Paris Salon, but now lost. The exploits of Napoleon and his army were popular subjects for French artists whose work was shown in official exhibitions.

   Anne-Louis Girodet de Roussy-Trioson · c. 1810 · Oil and ink on paper, laid down on canvas · nineteenth century
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/152851

   La obra es un boceto preparatorio para una pintura monumental que representa un momento sangriento de la invasión de Egipto por Napoleón en 1798, específicamente la supresión de un levantamiento en El Cairo. [1]
   La pintura celebra el punto de vista francés de la batalla y muestra elementos de lujo y brutalidad en la escena, incluyendo turbantes árabes, telas lujosas y sangre. [1]
   La escena representa un conflicto bélico con una fuerte carga dramática y violencia, lo que la hace una escena de batalla en la pintura francesa.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “This is a preparatory sketch for a monumental painting depicting one of the bloodiest moments of Napoleon’s 1798 invasion of Egypt: the suppression of an uprising in Cairo. The conflict included a massacre in the Al-Azhar Mosque of Mamelukes, a military class of enslaved men who occupied much of the Middle East at that time. As there were no surviving eyewitness reports, Girodet was free to interpret the event as he wished, and, as a commission from Napoleon, the painting celebrates the French point of view. Throughout the work, Girodet perpetuates European fantasies of the Middle East as simultaneously opulent and brutal, lavishing attention on Arab and Ottoman turbans, luxurious fabrics, bare flesh, and gore.”

3. **The Combat of the Giaour and Hassan**
   Eugène Delacroix · 1826 · Oil on canvas · 19th century
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/110663

   La pintura representa una escena violenta y frenética inspirada en un poema romántico que muestra un combate entre guerreros, uno de ellos llamado Giaour. [1]
   Aunque la escena es un combate entre guerreros, no se menciona que sea una batalla militar francesa ni que tenga relación con Francia o Napoleón.

   No hay información suficiente para confirmar que esta obra representa una escena de batalla en la pintura francesa.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “For this frenetic scene, Eugène Delacroix took inspiration from “The Giaour,” a poem in a popular series of romantic tales by the celebrated English poet Lord Byron. Giaour is a derogatory Turkish word for a Christian or non-Muslim applied here to the warrior at left clad in swirling white drapery. Amid a violent struggle, the Giaour is avenging the death of his lover at the hands of his opponent. Delacroix mirrored the two central figures and their horses as the Giaour is about to strike the fatal blow against the faceless Turk Hassan. The artist’s mastery of color is exemplified by his use of shimmering primary hues, while the loose handling of paint creates the sense of dynamism Delacroix was so capable of executing.
This painting reflects Delacroix’s sustained engagement with Orientalism, the artistic representation of non-European people and places, especially North Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. Delacroix was among the first European artists to travel to Africa when he visited Morocco in 1832, shortly after he completed this painting. Widespread in the nineteenth century, Orientalism was regularly leveraged to reinforce French colonial enterprises through often fantastical, violent, or erotic depictions of the customs and cultures of faraway locales.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/110663 · CC BY 4.0

Instrumentando en el **`EjecutorDeEtapas`**, que es el lugar que ese mismo recuadro señala, **sí hay latencia para las ocho**. la latencia por etapa deja de estar sobre-prometido. **Va reportado.**

nota_de_a8_vs_bd4: 🔴 **Las dos lecturas del libro mayor, y son proyecciones del mismo dato**: la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura pide el costo *por etapa* y la atribución de cada llamada a su rol atribuye *por rol, no al nombre de la etapa. En C1–C3 son **1:1**; en C4 el reranker es **N llamadas de un rol y una etapa** y `embedding_texto` es **un rol en dos etapas**. `libro_mayor` agrupa por rol —que sigue siendo la atribución de registro, declarada por el binding— y `libro_mayor_por_etapa` por la etapa en que el span corrió, **derivada del árbol de trazas y no de un parámetro**. nota_de_identidad: Clase 2 (la tabla de identidades): *registro de una ejecución*. La identidad fija **las entradas, no la salida** —una salida no determinista con la misma entrada es el dato que el muestreo fijado, registrado y con su variabilidad medida mide—, así que lleva **ordinal** y la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica. nota_de_la_tabla: degradación/la regla de qué corridas agregan a la tabla: una corrida con degradación **no planificada** no agrega a la tabla C0–C4 —*una C4 que degradó en silencio entraría etiquetada como C4 comportándose como C3*— y una con degradación **planificada** tampoco: es el criterio de respuesta garantizada y se reporta aparte.
